title: Identity Disclosure
description: The wearable device (Process P1) shares raw sensor telemetry data (heart rate, step counts, GPS position, timestamps) with the external entity (User/EE1). This act of sharing causes the threat because the external entity can link or identify the user based on the unique identifiers in the telemetry data.
assumptions: The wearable device is accessible to the external entity.

title: Data-Linking via Meta-Data
description: The data flow (DF1) transmits meta-data about the parties involved (e.g., device ID, user ID, timestamp) in transit. This data-centric threat arises because the external entity can use this metadata to link or identify the user, even if the raw telemetry data is not directly visible.
assumptions: The device transmits identifiable metadata (e.g., user ID, device ID) in the data stream.

title: Data Processing/Storage
description: The wearable device (Process P1) processes the incoming sensor telemetry data, potentially storing it or using it for device functionality. This action causes the threat because the device may retain or process the user's sensitive health data.
assumptions: The device processes the incoming sensor telemetry data.

title: Data Disclosure
description: Device (P1) shares personal data (exercise sessions, GPS traces, device id, timestamps) with the Companion Mobile App (P2) via the data flow DF2. This constitutes a data disclosure as the device transfers personal data to a third party (the app) without a direct data store intermediary, fitting the definition of transfer to a known or unknown third party.
assumptions: The data is considered personal data as it includes GPS traces and device identifiers.

title: Linking via Meta-data
description: The data flow DF2 transmits meta-data about the parties involved (e.g., device ID, timestamps, exercise session IDs) in transit. This meta-data can be used to link or identify the specific individuals whose data is being shared, constituting a data-centric threat.
assumptions: The app and device are identifiable by the metadata fields included in the sync.

title: Data Disclosure
description: The Companion Mobile App (P2) receives the sensor batches and processes them, potentially storing or using the personal data (exercise sessions, GPS traces, device id, timestamps) in a way that causes a threat. This is a data disclosure as the app processes the data.
assumptions: The app stores or uses the data in a manner that exposes it to unauthorized access or misuse.

title: Unawareness as a user sharing personal data
description: The user (ExternalEntity EE1) does not need to be the data subject for the data to be processed. The user is merely a 'wearer' of the app and does not have direct control over the data they share, leading to a potential privacy breach if the app processes personal data without explicit consent.
assumptions: The user is unaware of the specific data being processed or the extent of their data usage.

title: Data-centric threat: Meta-data about the parties being used to link or identify them
description: The data flow DF3 involves the companion mobile app (Process P2) receiving data from the user (ExternalEntity EE1). The meta-data about the parties (User and Companion App) being used to link or identify them could be used to track the user's activity or profile, creating a data-centric threat.
assumptions: The data flow involves the transfer of personal data (calorie intake, meals, weight) to a third-party process.

title: Data-centric threat: Processing data in a way that causes the threat
description: The companion mobile app (Process P2) receives the user's data and processes it. The processing of personal data (calorie intake, meals, weight) by the app could cause a privacy threat if the app stores, uses, or discards the data in a way that violates the user's privacy rights.
assumptions: The app processes the data without proper safeguards or user consent.

title: Data Disclosure
description: The mobile app (Process P2) directly writes health log data (calorie intake, weight history, exercise sessions) to the Health Log Store (DataStore DS1). This constitutes a data disclosure as the transfer of personal health data across a boundary to a third party (the store).

title: Data in Transit
description: Health log data is transmitted via the data flow (DF4) between the Process and the DataStore. The data-centric threat arises from the potential for meta-data about the parties being used to link or identify the data recipients, potentially compromising privacy.

title: Data Disclosure
description: The Health Log Store (DataStore DS1) receives the health log data and stores it. The threat arises at the destination where the data is processed and stored, potentially leading to further disclosure or unauthorized access.

title: Data Disclosure
description: The process (P2) writes GPS location traces with timestamps to the data store (DS2). This constitutes a data disclosure as the process transfers personal data (GPS location traces) to a third party (the data store).
assumptions: The data store is a known third party.

title: Data Disclosure
description: The data flow (DF5) transmits GPS location traces with timestamps in transit. The data-centric threat arises from the meta-data about the parties being used to link or identify the data recipients.
assumptions: The data flow carries metadata that could be used to identify the data recipients.

title: Data Disclosure
description: The data store (DS2) receives the GPS location traces with timestamps. The destination element (DS2) processes or stores the data in a way that causes the threat, as it may retain or use the data for its own purposes.
assumptions: The data store retains or uses the data for its own purposes.

title: Data Disclosure
description: The Health Log Store (DS1) shares personal health data (calorie, weight, exercise logs) with the Health Analytics Service (P3) for health-condition analysis. This constitutes a data disclosure as the data is transferred across a boundary to a third party (the analytics service) for processing.
assumptions: The data is considered personal health information as it relates to health conditions.

title: Linking/Identification Threat
description: The data flow (DF6) carries meta-data about the parties involved (DS1 and P3) that could be used to link or identify the individuals whose health data is being transmitted. This is a data-centric threat where the mere existence of the data flow itself enables identification.
assumptions: The data flow contains metadata that could be used to identify the data subjects.

title: Data Disclosure
description: The Health Analytics Service (P3) receives the health data and processes it for health-condition analysis. This processing action may lead to the disclosure of the data to third parties or for purposes beyond the intended health analysis, constituting a data disclosure.
assumptions: The processing of the data for health-condition analysis may result in further sharing or disclosure.

title: Data Disclosure
description: The data store (DS2) shares location history data with the Health Analytics Service (P3). This constitutes a data disclosure as the transfer of personal data across a boundary. The minimality principle is key: only strictly required personal data should be shared. If the data store is not confident that the analytics service will use this data for the intended purpose (deriving daily routine and movement patterns) without additional processing, this could be an implicit disclosure risk.
assumptions: The data store assumes the analytics service will use the data for the stated purpose.
uncertainty_note: Uncertain if the analytics service will use the data for the stated purpose without additional processing.

title: Linking Threat
description: The data flow (DF7) carries location history data in transit. If the data store or the analytics service uses meta-data about the parties (e.g., IP addresses, device IDs, or session identifiers) to link or identify the data subjects, this creates a linking threat. This is a data-centric threat where the data itself is used to identify the parties.
assumptions: The data store or analytics service uses meta-data to link or identify the data subjects.
uncertainty_note: Uncertain if meta-data is used to link or identify the data subjects.

title: Data Disclosure
description: The health analytics service (P3) receives the location history data and processes it to derive daily routine and movement patterns. If the service stores or shares this derived data (e.g., aggregated movement patterns) with a third party or stores it in a way that causes a threat, this constitutes a data disclosure. The minimality principle applies: only the derived patterns should be shared, not the raw location history.
assumptions: The analytics service stores or shares the derived patterns with a third party or stores them in a way that causes a threat.
uncertainty_note: Uncertain if the derived patterns are shared or stored in a way that causes a threat.

title: Profiling a group of individuals
description: The Health Analytics Service (P3) processes health-condition risk indicators and routine summaries, which are personal data related to specific data subjects. By aggregating these indicators, the service infers insights about a larger group of individuals (e.g., users with similar health profiles), constituting a profiling threat. This is a Linking threat where data of a single individual leads to insights about a larger group.
assumptions: The aggregated data is used to create group-level profiles.

title: Identifying the data subject
description: The Companion Mobile App (P2) receives the inferred health insights from P3. The threat arises at the destination because the app processes this data to provide personalized health recommendations or notifications. The act of processing this data to identify the specific user (or group) receiving the insights constitutes an Identifying threat.
assumptions: The app uses the insights to personalize the user experience.

title: Unauthorized Access to Dashboard Data
description: The process (P2) shares aggregated trend and condition indicator data (eating-disorder or diabetes risk signals) to the external entity (EE1). This constitutes a data disclosure threat where the process exposes sensitive health-related information without appropriate access controls or encryption.
assumptions: The process assumes that the dashboard data is accessible to the user or intended for them.

title: Data Linking and Identification Risk
description: The data flow (DF9) transmits metadata about the parties involved (the Companion Mobile App and the User) in transit. This meta-data could be used to link or identify the user, potentially compromising privacy if the metadata is not adequately anonymized or encrypted.
assumptions: The flow transmits metadata about the parties being used to link or identify them.

title: Unauthorized Processing or Storage
description: The destination element (EE1) receives and processes the data. There is a risk that the user (or the app) could misinterpret or mishandle the inferred condition indicators (eating-disorder or diabetes risk signals), leading to incorrect health decisions or data misuse.
assumptions: The destination element processes or stores the data in a way that causes the threat.

title: Data Disclosure
description: The Health Analytics Service (P3) shares personal health data and location information with the Cloud Hosting Provider (EE2). This constitutes a data disclosure as the data is transferred across a boundary to a third party.
assumptions: The data transfer is intended and designed as part of the service's replication and hosting capabilities.

title: Data in Transit
description: Data-centric threats arise during the transfer of the health analytics data and location dataset between the source (P3) and the destination (EE2). The data in transit may be used to link or identify the parties involved in the transfer.
assumptions: The data is transmitted via standard network protocols.

title: Data Disclosure
description: The Cloud Hosting Provider (EE2) receives and stores the health analytics data and location dataset. This storage and processing of personal data by a third party constitutes a data disclosure.
assumptions: The provider stores the data for the purpose of hosting and replicating the service.
